title: Describe Your Experience with Evidence
summary: Explain what you built, why it mattered and what you can actually prove.
prerequisites: At least one piece of work you have actually completed.
learningObjectives: Keep the scope of measurements clear.

sections.heading: Start with a specific piece of work
body: An experience statement is useful when another person can understand your responsibility. “Worked with Salesforce” names a platform but says little about your work. “Built a test-drive request form that validates the vehicle and records the customer’s chosen time” describes a feature someone can discuss with you.

Use three kinds of evidence carefully. Commercial work comes from a real employment or client context. A personal project is work you designed and completed yourself. A guided exercise follows a learning path. All three can demonstrate knowledge, but they are different contexts. Label the Northstar project as a training project unless you have separately delivered it for a real business.

callouts.text: A precise training example is more useful than an impressive claim that you cannot explain. It also gives the interviewer a clear starting point.

sections.heading: Build a short explanation from five parts
body: Write the situation, the requirement, your contribution, the result and how you checked it. For Northstar, the situation is that salespeople need a consistent way to request test drives. The requirement is to capture a customer, an available vehicle and a time. Your contribution might be the validation logic and its tests. The result is an implemented feature. Your evidence is a repeatable test and a short demonstration.

Be exact about ownership. If another learner designed the data model and you wrote the LWC, say that. If you extended a supplied starter class, identify the extension. This does not weaken the account; it shows that you understand the boundary of your responsibility. Avoid describing every part of a team project as something you personally delivered.

codeBlocks.caption: Reusable working prompt or template
codeBlocks.code:
Context: [the process or problem]
Requirement: [the behaviour needed]
My contribution: [what I personally changed]
Result: [what happened, with evidence]
Verification: [how I checked it]
Limitations: [what I did not implement or measure]

sections.heading: Use measurements only when you have them
body: A result does not have to contain a percentage. “Handles a test batch of 200 records without queries inside the loop” is a concrete technical result if you ran that test. “Improved sales productivity by 40%” is not supported merely because your form takes fewer clicks in a demonstration. Business impact needs a suitable baseline, a measurement period and a way to connect the change to the observation.

If you have a measurement, keep its scope. A local test that falls from 800 milliseconds to 300 milliseconds does not prove that production response times improved by the same amount. Explain the environment, the sample and the limitation. If you did not measure an outcome, describe what the feature enables and how you verified its behaviour instead of inventing a metric.

callouts.text: Do not turn a test result, estimate or expected benefit into a measured commercial outcome.

sections.heading: Prepare a short and a detailed version
body: Write a three-sentence version for a CV or introduction, then a two-minute version for an interview. The short version should name the feature, your work and the evidence. The longer version should add one difficulty, one decision and one limitation. Practice both without reading the text word for word.

For example: “I built a Salesforce training application for test-drive requests. I implemented bulk-safe validation and tests for unavailable vehicles and mixed valid and invalid records. I can demonstrate the behaviour in a development org; I have not deployed it for a real dealership.” That explanation gives the interviewer useful questions to ask without creating a false impression of production experience.

callouts.text: Ask a peer to identify your contribution and your evidence after hearing the explanation once. If they cannot, simplify it.

exercise.title: Apply this to your own search
exercise.brief: Write two evidence-based accounts: one completed feature and one problem you investigated.
steps: Identify the context and your exact contribution.
Collect an authorised code example, test result or demonstration.
Write a three-sentence summary and a two-minute account.
Underline every measurement and check its source.
Add one limitation that you can discuss honestly.
acceptance: The reader can distinguish your work from the team’s or starter project’s work.
Every number has a measurement source and scope.
Training work is labelled and still explains a meaningful technical result.

knowledgeCheck.question: Must every CV achievement include a percentage?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. A verified capability or technical result is useful; an invented percentage is misleading.

knowledgeCheck.question: How should you describe a tutorial extension?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Name the guided starting point and explain the part you changed independently.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why include a limitation?
knowledgeCheck.answer: It makes the boundary of your evidence clear and creates a realistic technical discussion.

recap: Keep the scope of measurements clear.

illustration.prompt: Create one landscape 16:9 lesson-cover illustration for SAM Salesforce Developer Studio. Restrained professional editorial illustration, flat geometric drawn forms with fine navy linework and a subtle paper texture. Warm ivory #F7F4EE, navy #12253C, muted cobalt #3867E8, restrained teal #138A86 and sage. One clear central scene, generous empty margins, at most three main visual groups. Calm adult learning design. Any people are clearly drawn stylized figures, never realistic photos. NO text, letters, numerals, logos, watermarks, Salesforce mascots, decorative clutter or glossy 3D. Exact topic: Experience Inventory. Subject: three concrete project artifacts connected to one personal contribution card.
